definition: To become less intense or widespread; to lessen or reduce something.
etymology: From Old French abatre "to beat down," from Latin ad- "to" + battuere "to beat" (also the source of "battle" and "batter").

examples.text: Wherever the sentiment of the majority is still genuine and intense, it is found to have abated little of its claim to be obeyed.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: Our institutions will not deteriorate by extension, and our sense of justice will not abate under tropic suns in distant seas.
examples.author: William McKinley

examples.text: Turkey pulled warships back from close escort of its Sismik 1 survey ship as the threat of conflict with Greece over oil rights in the Aegean Sea abated.
examples.source: Reuters, “Turkey Lifts Survey Ship Escort As Tension Abates”

definition: Difficult to understand; obscure.
etymology: From Latin abstrusus "concealed," past participle of abstrudere "to thrust away, hide."

examples.text: In a thousand ways he smoothed for me the path of knowledge and made the most abstruse inquiries clear and facile to my apprehension.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: The Golden Dustman seeming to be engaged in some abstruse calculation, Mr Wegg assisted him with the following additional items.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And this is incident to none but those, that converse in questions of matters incomprehensible, as the Schoole-men; or in questions of abstruse Philosophy.
examples.author: Thomas Hobbes

definition: The ability to make good judgments and quick, accurate decisions, especially in a particular field.
etymology: From Latin acumen "a point, sharpness," from acuere "to sharpen." The same root gives "acute" and "acupuncture."

examples.text: For a man who was never in the country, and who did not evidently do much in the way of business, his knowledge and acumen were wonderful.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: When they went down, uncle Pullet observed, with some acumen, that he reckoned the missis had been showing her bonnet,—that was what had made them so long upstairs.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: But when St. John had mused a few moments he recommenced as imperturbably and with as much acumen as ever.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: To warn or reprimand someone firmly, often gently but earnestly; to advise against something.
etymology: From Latin admonere "to remind, warn," from ad- "to" + monere "to warn" (compare "monitor").

examples.text: The President again briefly, but impressively, admonished him to answer only what was asked, and not to go off into irrelevant exclamations.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: She simply continued to be mild in her temper, inflexible in her judgment, disposed to admonish her husband, and able to frustrate him by stratagem.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Other considerations of the highest importance admonish us to cherish our Union and to cling to the Government which supports it.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: Brisk and cheerful readiness; eager willingness to do something.
etymology: From Latin alacritas, from alacer "lively, brisk."

examples.text: And the archdeacon scrubbed his hands and rubbed his face with a violent alacrity, which showed that Arabin's coming was a great point gained.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Some of the boys about me put in their claim not to be forgotten in the distribution of the good things, as I got out of my seat with great alacrity.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Emma was rather in dismay when only half a minute afterwards he began to speak of other things, and in a voice of the greatest alacrity and enjoyment.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: To make something bad or unsatisfactory better.
etymology: From French améliorer, from Latin melior "better."

examples.text: The work of ameliorating the conditions of life—the true civilizing process that makes life more and more secure—had gone steadily on to a climax.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: I sought to improve her manners and ameliorate her general tone; she (supported in this likewise by her relations) resented my endeavours.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Spring drew on: she was indeed already come; the frosts of winter had ceased; its snows were melted, its cutting winds ameliorated.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

definition: Something that belongs or seems to belong to another time, especially something conspicuously old-fashioned.
etymology: From Greek anakhronismos, from ana- "backward, against" + khronos "time."

examples.text: "You are too young—it is an anachronism for you to have such thoughts," said Will, energetically, with a quick shake of the head habitual to him.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: This was what he required a steamer for, and I knew he was just then negotiating enthusiastically with a Parsee firm for an old, brig-rigged, sea-anachronism of ninety horse-power.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: 'Our ancestors had no great tolerance for anachronisms.'
examples.author: H. G. Wells

definition: Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected.
etymology: From Greek anōmalia "unevenness," from an- "not" + homalos "even."

examples.text: Even to-day the masses of the Negroes see all too clearly the anomalies of their position and the moral crookedness of yours.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: I must say that I had my doubts about the strict justice of this, and was not even frightened out of them by the bushel of wheat which reconciles all anomalies.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Rainbow chairman Allan Hawkins said in a statement, "In our opinion BIL have deliberately tried to create anomalies in the market prices of Rainbow and Progressive shares since the merger was announced."
examples.source: Reuters, “Rainbow Says Brierley Upsetting Progressive Merger”

definition: A deep-seated feeling of dislike or aversion.
etymology: From Greek antipatheia, from anti- "against" + pathos "feeling."

examples.text: But I am not really Mrs. Richard Phillotson, but a woman tossed about, all alone, with aberrant passions, and unaccountable antipathies...
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Ever since the fatal night, the end of my labours, and the beginning of my misfortunes, I had conceived a violent antipathy even to the name of natural philosophy.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: And the invocation was uttered in such a tone as to indicate a rooted antipathy to anything so commonplace, even if she had not added that sequins gave her the sick.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern.
etymology: From Greek apatheia, from a- "without" + pathos "feeling." The Stoics used it approvingly, for freedom from passion.

examples.text: Charlotte had seen her brother's apathy, when he neglected to follow Mrs. Bold out of the room, with anger which she could hardly suppress.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He had had full warning of Mr. Flack's intentions, and might have bought the plot before building commenced: but he was apathetic and dilatory.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: Now we need to focus on giving young people, especially young men in our cities, better options than apathy, or gangs, or jail.
examples.author: George W. Bush

definition: To pacify or placate someone by giving in to their demands.
etymology: From Old French apaisier "to bring to peace," from a pais "to peace," from Latin pax.

examples.text: Provocations to produce the desired appearances might even be given to some foreign power, and appeased again by timely concessions.
examples.author: Hamilton

examples.text: Together, we have resisted the trap of appeasement, cynicism, and isolation that gives temptation to tyrants.
examples.author: George H. W. Bush

examples.text: The White House aide said of the tariff action, "it wasn't done to appease Congress, but because there was an unfair trade practice."
examples.source: Reuters, “Japanese Tariffs Seen As Worldwide Warning”

definition: Enthusiastic or passionate; burning with feeling.
etymology: From Latin ardere "to burn" (also in "arson").

examples.text: There is a bright-eyed woman, of a strong will and immense power of business detail, who throws herself into objects with surprising ardour!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: For all his ardent reading, and his ardent life, was he anything but a small-town youth bred on an illiberal farm and in cheap tailor shops?
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The arrangement should be such as to put at the command of the Government the ardent patriotism and youthful vigor of the country.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: Involving or requiring strenuous effort; difficult and tiring.
etymology: From Latin arduus "steep, high, difficult."

examples.text: Archie Ruthvel had just come in, and, as his story goes, was about to begin his arduous day by giving a dressing-down to his chief clerk.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: If I do not sink under the weight of this deep conviction it is because I find some support in a consciousness of the purposes and a confidence in the principles which I bring with me into this arduous service.
examples.author: James Madison

examples.text: Producers and consumers could not find common ground on the issue of quota distribution in eight days of arduous, often heated talks, delegates said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ico Council Ends In Failure To Agree Quotas”

definition: Characterized by severe self-discipline and abstention from indulgence; a person who lives this way.
etymology: From Greek askētikos, from askētēs "monk, hermit," originally "one who exercises, an athlete," from askein "to exercise, train."

examples.text: He had known its place for years, and made no effort to find it, even before his new ascetic creed had cut him off from property or pleasures.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: With her large brown eyes, thin, ascetic face, her pale skin, and broad forehead, she might have stepped out of a picture by Burne-Jones.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: It was revived among us towards the end of last century by one of the great "ascetics," as they called him, Paissy Velitchkovsky, and his disciples.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To make an unpleasant feeling less intense; to satisfy an appetite or desire.
etymology: From Old French assouagier, from Latin ad- "to" + suavis "sweet."

examples.text: I cannot deny that I grieved for his grief, whatever that was, and would have given much to assuage it.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Philip discovered that the greatest tragedy of life to these people was not separation or death, that was natural and the grief of it could be assuaged with tears, but loss of work.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Sometimes his spirit would rise, a dark spot would show itself on his cheek, and he would rebel, but Charlotte would assuage him with some peculiar triumph of her culinary art and all again would be smooth for awhile.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Showing a willingness to take bold risks; sometimes, showing impudent lack of respect.
etymology: From Latin audax "bold," from audere "to dare."

examples.text: War rages yet with the audacious Boythorn, though at uncertain intervals, and now hotly, and now coolly, flickering like an unsteady fire.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She is, therefore, always, woman-like, a lover of young men, because they are less cautious, more violent, and with more audacity command her.
examples.author: Niccolò Machiavelli (tr. W. K. Marriott)

examples.text: Happily, the human mind is so constituted that no party can reach to the audacity of doing this.
examples.author: Abraham Lincoln

definition: Severe or strict in manner or attitude; having no comforts or luxuries; plain.
etymology: From Greek austēros "harsh, bitter," originally describing a taste that makes the tongue dry.

examples.text: He had, without explanation, the impression of a slaggy cliff and on it, in silhouette against menacing clouds, a lone and austere figure.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: I looked back at the platform when we had left it far behind and saw the tall, austere figure of Holmes standing motionless and gazing after us.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: The revaluation formed part of a new go-it-alone economic strategy which Kaunda adopted to replace Zambia's IMF austerity program.
examples.source: Reuters, “Zambia Cuts Prices As Troops Patrol Copperbelt”

definition: So lacking in originality as to be obvious and boring.
etymology: From French banal, originally "compulsory, common to all" — relating to a feudal ban, the facilities a lord required tenants to use. "Shared by everyone" drifted to "commonplace."

examples.text: And when the remark comes it's always something he has seen or felt for himself—never a bit banal THAT would be what one might have feared and what would kill me But never.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: She promised to meet him in Deauville, the coming summer, "though," she sighed, "it's becoming too dreadfully banal; nothing but Americans and frowsy English baronesses."
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: They hurt each other very much, and sometimes they were close to weeping, and invariably he used banal phrases about her duties and she used phrases quite as banal about freedom, and through it all, her discovery that she really could get away from Main Street was as sweet as the discovery of love.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: To give a false impression of something; to contradict or show to be false.
etymology: Old English belēogan "to deceive by lying," from be- + lēogan "to lie."

examples.text: Their full slow eyes belied the words, the gestures eager and unoffending, but knew the rancours massed about them and knew their zeal was vain.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: And it is impossible for me to say that Mr. Irwine was altogether belied by the generic classification assigned him.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Four years of new experience have not belied our historic instinct.
examples.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

definition: Well meaning and kindly; serving a charitable rather than profit-making purpose.
etymology: From Latin bene "well" + volens "wishing," from velle "to wish."

examples.text: I know no man more likely than Mr. Knightley to do the sort of thing—to do any thing really good-natured, useful, considerate, or benevolent.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Is it not (we may ask these projectors in politics) the true interest of all nations to cultivate the same benevolent and philosophic spirit?
examples.author: Hamilton

examples.text: If national pride is ever justifiable or excusable it is when it springs, not from power or riches, grandeur or glory, but from conviction of national innocence, information, and benevolence.
examples.author: John Adams

definition: To support or strengthen; to prop up.
etymology: Old English bolster "long pillow, cushion." The verb sense "prop up," as with a pillow, dates from the 1500s.

examples.text: Prince Andrew answered all his questions reluctantly but reasonably, and then said he wanted a bolster placed under him as he was uncomfortable and in great pain.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: So, we must prepare for peace not only by reducing weapons but by bolstering prosperity, liberty, and democracy however and wherever we can.
examples.author: Ronald Reagan

examples.text: Miller's remarks reflected concern that the U.S. central bank might feel compelled to tighten credit as a means of bolstering the dollar.
examples.source: Reuters, “Budget Chief Miller Warns Fed On Interest Rates”

definition: To begin to grow or increase rapidly; to flourish.
etymology: From Old French burjon "a bud, shoot," so the first sense was "to put forth buds."

examples.text: Mother's milk, Purefoy, the milk of human kin, milk too of those burgeoning stars overhead rutilant in thin rainvapour, punch milk, such as those rioters will quaff in their guzzling den, milk of madness, the honeymilk of Canaan's land.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: The major responsibility for development in these fields rests in the localities, even though the Federal Government will continue to do its proper part in meeting the genuine needs of a burgeoning population.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

examples.text: Burgeoning imports of microwave ovens and of frozen Coquilles St Jacques will be restricted by a strict application of French quality standards — something EC states say often happens to their own exports entering Japan.
examples.source: Reuters, “Trade Issues Straining Ec'S Patience With Japan”

definition: Given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behavior.
etymology: From Italian capriccio "a sudden start," popularly linked with capra "goat," as if moving with a goat's unpredictable leaps.

examples.text: After sipping a dozen spoonfuls of tea, he suddenly released his head, pushed the spoon away capriciously, and sank back on the pillow.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: And all this was to have come without study or other inconvenience, purely by the favor of providence in the shape of an old gentleman's caprice.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: But the next morning when he awoke he felt rather vexed with her, and decided that she was rather unreasonable, not to say capricious.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

definition: To reprimand someone severely.
etymology: From Latin castigare "to correct, punish," from castus "pure" (also the source of "chaste").

examples.text: She was in a very paroxysm of self-castigation, and, concluding, she looked with defiant resolution at the elder.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: "I suppose," observes Volumnia, having taken a little time to recover her spirits after her late castigation, "I suppose Mr. Tulkinghorn has been worked to death."
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But ultimately this little castigation had broken no bones between him and his friend Mr. Towers.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Able to burn or corrode organic tissue by chemical action; sarcastic in a scathing and bitter way.
etymology: From Greek kaustikos "capable of burning," from kaiein "to burn" (also in "cauterize").

examples.text: Mr Flintwinch, after scraping his chin, and looking about with caustic disparagement of the Pig-Market, nodded to Arthur, and followed.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: His—if I may say so—his caustic placidity, and, at the same time, his intelligent sympathy with Jim's aspirations, appealed to me.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The latter in Pierre's presence had ceased to be caustic, and his face expressed perplexity as to what Julie's smile might mean.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
etymology: From Latin cogere "to compel," from co- "together" + agere "to drive."

examples.text: The third, and most cogent reason for restricting the interference of government, is the great evil of adding unnecessarily to its power.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: The more attentively I consider and investigate the reasons which appear to have given birth to this opinion, the more I become convinced that they are cogent and conclusive.
examples.author: Hamilton

examples.text: Caesar gave way before such cogent reasoning, and the cardinals were consequently invited to dinner.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Showing smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements.
etymology: From Latin complacere "to please very much." In the 1600s it meant simply "pleasing"; the sense of smugness came later.

examples.text: Sir Leicester sits in my Lady's room—that room in which Mr. Tulkinghorn read the affidavit in Jarndyce and Jarndyce—particularly complacent.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: History and experience tells us that moral progress cannot come in comfortable and in complacent times, but out of trial and out of confusion.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

examples.text: "We must never be complacent and we must always be very watchful, but I think we would be very expensive," he said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Allied-Lyons Sees Substantial Second Half Growth”

definition: Intended or likely to placate or pacify.
etymology: From Latin conciliare "to bring together, unite," from concilium "council."

examples.text: Elizabeth disdained the appearance of noticing this civil reflection, but its meaning did not escape, nor was it likely to conciliate her.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: When I became President only 5 months ago, I promised the last Congress a policy of communication, conciliation, compromise, and cooperation.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

examples.text: Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone sounded a conciliatory note in Japan's increasingly bitter row with the United States over trade in computer microchips.
examples.source: Reuters, “Nakasone Sounds Conciliatory Note In Chip Dispute”

definition: To confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding.
etymology: From Latin corroborare "to strengthen," from com- + robur "strength, oak" (also in "robust").

examples.text: This was corroborated by his landlord, who had received by messenger the key of the house together with the rent due, in English money.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: I mention it now, only as a corroboration (though I hope it may be needless) of my being free from the sordid design attributed to me.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: To doubt any longer was impossible; there was the evidence of the senses, and ten thousand persons who came to corroborate the testimony.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

definition: Having or showing too great a readiness to believe things.
etymology: From Latin credulus "trusting," from credere "to believe" (also in "credit" and "creed").

examples.text: For she is credulous and good-hearted, and she believes everything from the goodness of her heart and... and... and she is like that... yes...
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: He who had been a boy very credulous of life was no longer greatly interested in the possible and improbable adventures of each new day.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Yet it is important to know that our patience at the bargaining table is nearly inexhaustible, though our credulity is limited that our hopes for peace are unfailing, while our determination to protect our security is resolute.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: Deserving blame.
etymology: From Latin culpabilis, from culpa "fault, blame," as in the phrase mea culpa.

examples.text: The conduct of those uninteresting people who managed the business of the world had been culpable just in the points most injurious to her in particular.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: If the resources which ought to have been devoted to them, had been diverted from them for the most prudent investment, the moral culpability would have been the same.
examples.author: John Stuart Mill

examples.text: For the first time in history the legal culpability of war makers is being determined.
examples.author: Harry S. Truman

definition: A scarcity or lack of something.
etymology: Middle English derthe, from dear in the old sense "costly" + the noun suffix -th. When food was dear, it was scarce.

examples.text: The dearth of strong moral character, of unbending righteousness, he felt, was their great shortcoming, and here he would begin.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: To sojourn in that land He comes, invited by a younger son In time of dearth, a son whose worthy deeds Raise him to be the second in that realm Of Pharaoh.
examples.author: John Milton

examples.text: And oh, this dearth of the human physiognomy! and, worse than all, the terrible intimation of Kenneth that I need not expect to be out of doors till spring!
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Humble submission and respect.
etymology: From French déférence, from déférer "to yield," from Latin deferre "to carry down, refer."

examples.text: He bowed with icy deference when my terms of eulogy were all exhausted, and silently opened the door for me to go out into the passage again.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: Governor and commander are interchangeable terms with Phil, expressive of the same respect and deference and applicable to nobody but Mr. George.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: If, on the other hand, we hang back in deference to local economic pressures, we will find ourselves cut off from our major allies.
examples.author: John F. Kennedy

definition: Causing harm or damage.
etymology: From Greek dēlētērios "noxious," from dēleisthai "to hurt, damage."

examples.text: Or might it suffice him that every wholesome growth should be converted into something deleterious and malignant at his touch?
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: He was a mournful dyspeptic, intent on finding out the deleterious ingredients of every dish and diverted from this care only by the sound of his wife's voice.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: The Captain continued that deleterious amusement of smoking, long after the inn and the street were gone to bed.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping from one thing to another.
etymology: From Latin desultorius "of a circus rider who leaps from horse to horse," from desilire "to leap down."

examples.text: Philip saw several fellows with a desultory, timid look dawdling around, and surmised that, like himself, they were there for the first time.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Hitherto he had found, in her presence and her talk, the aesthetic amusement which a reflective man is apt to seek in desultory intercourse with pretty women.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Then they spoke of other things—the desultory talk of those who have been fighting to reach one another, and whose reward is to rest quietly in each other's arms.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Intended to teach, particularly in having moral instruction as an ulterior motive; sometimes, overly preachy.
etymology: From Greek didaktikos "apt at teaching," from didaskein "to teach."

examples.text: On many nights those passing by his little back garden might hear his high, didactic voice laying down the law to men and particularly to women.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: She sent this didactic gem to several markets, but it found no purchaser, and she was inclined to agree with Mr. Dashwood that morals didn't sell.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

examples.text: "And the more there is of 'em, the more they must love one another," Mrs. Moss went on, looking at her children with a didactic purpose.
examples.author: George Eliot

definition: Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence.
etymology: From Latin diffidere "to mistrust," from dis- "not" + fidere "to trust." To lack trust in oneself.

examples.text: At the class-dinner he had seen poor Overbrook, in a shiny blue serge business-suit, being diffident in a corner with three other failures.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: Every time their eyes met, I saw more and more what a tremendous power that weak, diffident school-girl could wield if she chose to do it.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: The same diffidence induces me to hope for instruction and aid from the coordinate branches of the Government, and for the indulgence and support of my fellow citizens generally.
examples.author: Andrew Jackson

definition: A person who cultivates an area of interest, such as the arts, without real commitment or knowledge.
etymology: From Italian dilettante "lover (of an art)," from dilettare "to delight." Originally a compliment; by the 1800s it implied superficiality.

examples.text: Surely we have wit enough to found a Negro college so manned and equipped as to steer successfully between the dilettante and the fool.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: The cottage was far from that standard at present, for Lisbeth's rheumatism had forced her to give up her old habits of dilettante scouring and polishing.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He had dawdled over his cigar because he was at heart a dilettante, and thinking over a pleasure to come often gave him a subtler satisfaction than its realisation.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: To regard or represent as being of little worth; to belittle.
etymology: From Old French desparagier "to marry someone of unequal rank," from des- "apart" + parage "equality of rank," from Latin par "equal."

examples.text: They paid high for poor accommodation, and disparaged a place while they pretended to like it: which was exactly the Marshalsea custom.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: It is not meet that I should make too disparaging comparisons between humdrum travel on a railway and that royal summer flight across a continent in a stagecoach.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: The dangerous antimilitary sentiment discouraged defense spending and unfairly disparaged the men and women who serve in our Armed Forces.
examples.author: Gerald Ford

definition: Essentially different in kind; not allowing comparison.
etymology: From Latin disparatus "separated," from dis- "apart" + parare "to prepare." Associated in English with dispar "unequal."

examples.text: I might have seen there was too great a disparity between the ages of the parties to make it likely that they were man and wife.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: 'There can be no disparity in marriage like unsuitability of mind and purpose'—'no disparity in marriage like unsuitability of mind and purpose.'
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: However, "differentiated policy treatment is required" to take account of large disparities in the situation around the EC, he said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Consensus Builds For World Agricultural Reform”

definition: To conceal one's true motives, feelings, or beliefs; to disguise or feign.
etymology: An alteration of Old French dessembler, influenced by "resemble"; from Latin dissimulare "to disguise."

examples.text: But in this, our last interview of friendship, I approached her with a sense of guilt that almost took from me the power of dissembling.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Yet without power to kill, or change, or shun the fact; he likewise knew that to mankind he did long dissemble; in some sort, did still.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: He told me his secret in a thousand ways because he could not dissemble, but he does not dream that he has told it.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: Inclined to lay down principles as undeniably true, without consideration of evidence or the opinions of others.
etymology: From Greek dogma "opinion, decree," from dokein "to seem good, think."

examples.text: Two thousand years ago such dogmatism, readily welcome, would have scouted the idea of blond races ever leading civilization.
examples.author: W. E. B. Du Bois

examples.text: His gentleness was never tinged by dogmatism, and his instructions were given with an air of frankness and good nature that banished every idea of pedantry.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: There is no subject of economic discussion so intricate and so likely to evoke differing views and dogmatic statements as this one.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: Cheerful and full of energy.
etymology: From Latin ebullire "to boil over," from e- "out" + bullire "to boil." High spirits bubbling over.

examples.text: The ebullient Poehl spent seven years in Bonn in top ministerial posts under the Social Democrats, now in opposition, before he moved to the Bundesbank.
examples.source: Reuters, “Poehl Looks Set For Eight More Years At Bundesbank”

examples.text: The data, which has provided not clear-cut view of the economy, coupled with dampened activity in the foreign exchange markets after the Paris initiative has made for "less than ebullient market action," Mains said.
examples.source: Reuters, “Trading Range Likely To Continue In Debt Futures”

examples.text: But a rare public row between the ebullient Poehl, president of the Bundesbank, and Stoltenberg, over a controversial investment tax proposal, has added to the woes of the country's already nervous financial markets, bankers said.
examples.source: Reuters, “German Financial Policy Makers In Rare Dissension”

definition: The ability to produce a desired or intended result.
etymology: From Latin efficacia, from efficere "to accomplish."

examples.text: The second answer is, that the existence of such a power in the Constitution will have a strong influence in giving efficacy to requisitions.
examples.author: Hamilton

examples.text: The devoutest person could have rendered no greater homage to the efficacy of an honest prayer than he did in this distrust of his wife.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But other dealers said they doubted the efficacy of central bank intervention, saying it may stimulate the dollar's decline because many dealers are likely to await such dollar buying intervention as a chance to sell dollars.
examples.source: Reuters, “Dollar Seen Falling Unless Japan Spurs Economy”

definition: Insolent or impertinent behavior; shameless boldness.
etymology: From French effronterie, from Late Latin effrons "shameless," from ex- "out" + frons "forehead." Barefaced, putting one's forehead forward.

examples.text: He was not in truth much surprised at Mr. Slope's effrontery, but he was obliged to act as though he had been to save his daughter's feelings.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: He stood close to her, and the effrontery in his eyes repelled the old, vanishing self in her, yet drew all her awakening sensuousness.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

examples.text: Some of those Medicis would have smuggled themselves in sure.—What they had not the effrontery to do, was not worth doing.
examples.author: Mark Twain

definition: Fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing; clearly expressive.
etymology: From Latin eloqui "to speak out," from e- "out" + loqui "to speak" (compare "loquacious").

examples.text: Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent an extremely long and characteristically eloquent letter in which he begged her to lend him three roubles.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It is the loved subject of all his evening discourses, the source of all his eloquence, the secret of all his power over the female heart.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: Their newly found economic strength is eloquent testimony to the striking success of the policies of economic cooperation which we and they have pursued.
examples.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower

definition: To match or surpass a person or achievement, typically by imitation.
etymology: From Latin aemulari "to rival," from aemulus "rivaling."

examples.text: I will endeavour, in my relations with Mrs. Merridew, to emulate the moderation which Betteredge displays in his relations with me.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: 'My son's great capacity was tempted on, there, by a feeling of voluntary emulation and conscious pride,' the fond lady went on to say.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: And we know that the best way to enhance freedom in other lands is to demonstrate here that our democratic system is worthy of emulation.
examples.author: Jimmy Carter

definition: To cause someone to feel drained of energy or vitality; to weaken. (It does not mean "energize.")
etymology: From Latin enervare "to weaken," literally "to remove the sinews," from e- "out" + nervus "sinew."

examples.text: Enervated, prostrate, and breathless, he became unconscious of outward objects; he seemed to be entering that vague delirium preceding death.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: If he possesses an unusual share of native energy, or the enervating magic of place do not operate too long upon him, his forfeited powers may be redeemable.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: An artful cabal in that council would be able to distract and to enervate the whole system of administration.
examples.author: Hamilton

definition: A person or thing that is mysterious, puzzling, or difficult to understand.
etymology: From Greek ainigma "riddle," from ainissesthai "to speak in riddles."

examples.text: Daniel felt the presence of a new guest who seemed to come with an enigmatic veiled face, and to carry dimly-conjectured, dreaded revelations.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: You see, my dear boy"—Madame Hohlakov suddenly looked arch and a charming, though enigmatic, smile played about her lips—"you see, I suspect...
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: I was at first unable to solve these questions, but perpetual attention and time explained to me many appearances which were at first enigmatic.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

definition: Lasting for a very short time.
etymology: From Greek ephēmeros "lasting only a day," from epi- "on" + hēmera "day."

examples.text: In fact, if there could be any hope, it would be very ephemeral, because there would be no claim for assistance in that case, far from it....
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: They talked on slight and ephemeral subjects, and when his tea was brought up he told the amazed little servant that a cup was to be set for Sue.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: Her beauty itself was not the mere ephemeral possession it might have been in the hands of inexperience: her skill in enhancing it, the care she took of it, the use she made of it, seemed to give it a kind of permanence.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Mental calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus "even" + animus "mind."

examples.text: And therefore he will be least likely to lament, and will bear with the greatest equanimity any misfortune of this sort which may befall him.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: An exhausted composure, a worn-out placidity, an equanimity of fatigue not to be ruffled by interest or satisfaction, are the trophies of her victory.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: But suddenly something happened which was very annoying and unpleasant for every one in the house, and completely upset Fyodor Pavlovitch's equanimity at once.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: To use ambiguous language so as to conceal the truth or avoid committing oneself.
etymology: From Late Latin aequivocare "to call by the same name," from aequus "equal" + vocare "to call."

examples.text: He made a curious grimace—one of his strange and equivocal demonstrations—threw down his cue and followed me from the room.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: Jos had always had rather a mean opinion of the Captain, and now began to think his courage was somewhat equivocal.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: The three who had risen fell away from Gogol, and that equivocal person himself resumed his seat.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

definition: Having or showing great knowledge or learning.
etymology: From Latin eruditus "instructed," from erudire "to polish," literally "to bring out of roughness," from e- "out" + rudis "rough, untrained" (compare "rude").

examples.text: He had never been fond of Mr. Casaubon, and if it had not been for the sense of obligation, would have laughed at him as a Bat of erudition.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: In fact, his disappointment at the nature of those tongues had, after a while, been the means of still further glorifying the erudition of Christminster.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: But I delivered this written communication (slate and all) with my own hand, and Joe received it as a miracle of erudition.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with specialized knowledge.
etymology: From Greek esōterikos "belonging to an inner circle," from esōterō "further in." First applied to Pythagorean teaching meant for initiates.

examples.text: The merchants valued him not less than we, his esoteric friends.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: Two marquees had been erected for these two banquets: that for the quality on the esoteric or garden side of a certain deep ha-ha; and that for the non-quality on the exoteric or paddock side of the same.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: The life esoteric is not for ordinary person.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.
etymology: From Latin exacerbare "to irritate," from ex- "thoroughly" + acerbus "harsh, bitter."

examples.text: Iran had warned the United States earlier in the day against exacerbating the Gulf crisis, saying military action would endanger American interests.
examples.source: Reuters, “Diplomats Call U.S. Attack On Oil Rig Restrained”

examples.text: In particular, he told an American Stock Exchange conference, a decline in the dollar below current levels would exacerbate financial market conditions.
examples.source: Reuters, “Fed'S Johnson Warns Against Lower Dollar”

examples.text: Iran warned the United States on Monday against exacerbating the Gulf crisis, saying it would endanger American interests.
examples.source: Reuters, “Iran Warns U.S. Against Raising Tension In Gulf”

definition: To show or declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing.
etymology: From Medieval Latin exculpare, from ex- "out of" + culpa "blame."

examples.text: She was helped home by poor Susan and treacherous Mrs. Betty, who, now the mischief was done, thought only of exculpating herself to her master.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: Two months passed away in hopeless expectation on my part, while I must do the magistrate the justice to say that he used every means to obtain information of the person I declared could exculpate me if he would.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: The bishop thought it necessary to exculpate himself.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

definition: To praise enthusiastically.
etymology: From Latin extollere "to raise up," from ex- "out, up" + tollere "to raise."

examples.text: I extolled her beauty, her gaiety, her wit, so warmly, that my praises excited in him a desire to see a damsel adorned by such attractions.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: Cousin,'—this to the poor relation, never wearied of extolling her patroness's charity—'he is getting a bloom on the skin of a new-curried horse.
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling

examples.text: As he had continued to look steadily at me, I took it as a reminder that he objected to being extolled for his consideration.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; very concerned about matters of cleanliness or taste.
etymology: From Latin fastidiosus "disdainful, squeamish," from fastidium "loathing."

examples.text: The count appeared, dressed with the greatest simplicity, but the most fastidious dandy could have found nothing to cavil at in his toilet.
examples.author: Alexandre Dumas (tr. anonymous (1846))

examples.text: Aye, I said, I knew all along that a fastidious gentleman like you would not be contented with the thoughts of other people about these matters.
examples.author: Plato (tr. Benjamin Jowett)

examples.text: She meant 'facinating', but as Grace didn't know the exact meaning of either word, fastidious sounded well and made a good impression.
examples.author: Louisa May Alcott

definition: Having or displaying a passionate intensity.
etymology: From Latin fervere "to boil, glow."

examples.text: How lovingly and fervently did it commend the pretty creature I had won, with all her artless graces best displayed, to my most gentle care!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Her jungle romance had faded, but she retained a religious fervor, a surge of half-formed thought about the creation of beauty by suggestion.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: And tonight I call on all our allies and peace-loving nations throughout the world to join us with renewed fervor in a global effort to combat terrorism.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

definition: Excessively talkative, especially on trivial matters.
etymology: From Latin garrulus, from garrire "to chatter."

examples.text: Disdaining the heroic outfit, excitable in her methods, garrulous, episodical, shrill, she misled her lover much as she had misled her aunt.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: Now and then came a flash of cockney humour, now and then some old lady, a character such as Charles Dickens might have drawn, would amuse them by her garrulous oddities.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: In this state of second childhood, it had an air of being in its own way garrulous about its early life.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Fond of company; sociable. (Of animals) living in flocks or herds.
etymology: From Latin gregarius, from grex "flock, herd" (also in "congregate" and "egregious").

examples.text: Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place for his habitual gregarious resort.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: The contrary instincts and inclinations now attain to moral honour, the gregarious instinct gradually draws its conclusions.
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: It was so that the gregarious animals had overcome the predaceous; it was so, in human history, that the people had mastered the kings.
examples.author: Upton Sinclair

definition: Sly or cunning intelligence.
etymology: From Old French guile "deceit," probably of Germanic origin, related to "wile."

examples.text: This guileless confectioner was not by any means sober, and had a black eye in the green stage of recovery, which was painted over.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: She looked on with some amusement.—Miss Bates's gratitude for Mrs. Elton's attentions to Jane was in the first style of guileless simplicity and warmth.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: She knew that he loved her—a frank, blustering fellow without guile enough to conceal his feelings, and no desire to do so.
examples.source: The Awakening and Selected Short Stories
examples.author: Kate Chopin

definition: A lengthy and aggressive speech; to lecture someone at length in an aggressive manner.
etymology: From Old French arenge, from Medieval Latin harenga, probably from a Germanic word for an assembly or a crowd.

examples.text: When Lebeziatnikov finished his long-winded harangue with the logical deduction at the end, he was quite tired, and the perspiration streamed from his face.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: But the venom of the chaplain's harangue had worked into his blood, and sapped the life of his sweet contentment.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: The schoolmaster was sitting at his high desk, with his back to me, apparently haranguing the pupils, who were all gathered together in front of him, with one exception.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Acting or done quickly and without thought or care.
etymology: From Latin impetus "attack, force," from impetere "to rush upon."

examples.text: She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to go to him, when light, impetuous, and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: With those words uttered impetuously, Will rose, put out his hand to Rosamond, still with the air of a somnambulist, and went away.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Then impetuously he told her that Mildred had left him and that his unhappiness had been so great that he almost killed himself.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition: Unable to be appeased or placated; relentless.
etymology: From Latin implacabilis, from in- "not" + placare "to appease" (compare "placate").

examples.text: Her iron-grey hair hung in heavy bands on either side of her face—her dark eyes looked straight forward, with a hard, defiant, implacable stare.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

examples.text: With these words, and a laugh, and laying a bitter stress on the word "ladyship," Mrs. Chadband folds her arms and looks implacably at Mr. Bucket.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Not a word more would he say, but sat in his implacable sullenness as indifferent to me as though I had not been in the room at all.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

definition: Not in harmony or keeping with the surroundings or other aspects of something.
etymology: From Latin incongruus, from in- "not" + congruus "agreeing."

examples.text: Obstacles, incongruities, all melted into the sense of completion with which his soul was flooded by this outward satisfaction of his longing.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: This stupid repetition was too incongruous in its ineptitude with the serious, brooding and enigmatic glance he turned upon his visitor.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The negative upon the acts of the legislative by the executive authority, and that in the hands of one individual, would seem to be an incongruity in our system.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Wanting to avoid activity or exertion; lazy.
etymology: From Late Latin indolens "not feeling pain," from in- "not" + dolere "to suffer." Painless became "taking no trouble."

examples.text: Eliza generally took no more notice of her sister's indolence and complaints than if no such murmuring, lounging object had been before her.
examples.author: Charlotte Brontë

examples.text: He was one of those, who, liking work, knew how to do it, and despite his indolence would sometimes spend a whole night at his writing table.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: When the first transports of rage which had produced his activity in seeking her were over, he naturally returned to all his former indolence.
examples.author: Jane Austen

definition: Too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.
etymology: From Latin ineffabilis, from in- "not" + effabilis "utterable," from effari "to speak out."

examples.text: It is an ineffably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm, after a prolonged squeezing, and subsequent decanting.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: Thus while God spake, ambrosial fragrance fill'd All Heaven, and in the blessed Spirits elect Sense of new joy ineffable diffus'd.
examples.author: John Milton

examples.text: Dunlop, Judge, the noblest Roman of them all, A.E., Arval, the Name Ineffable, in heaven hight: K.H., their master, whose identity is no secret to adepts.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Impossible to stop or prevent; (of a person) impossible to persuade.
etymology: From Latin inexorabilis, from in- "not" + exorare "to prevail upon by entreaty," from orare "to pray."

examples.text: If he was by an inexorable logic to pay for it he was literally impatient to know the cost, and he held himself ready to pay in instalments.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: A third challenge we have is to keep this inexorable march of technology from giving terrorists and potentially hostile nations the means to undermine our defenses.
examples.author: Bill Clinton

examples.text: However, in the face of sterling's apparently inexorable climb, the authorities today decided to cede to pressure and allow a half-point cut.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.K. Issues One Billion Stg Bond Tranche”

definition: Innocent, unsuspecting, and candid. (Do not confuse with ingenious, "clever.")
etymology: From Latin ingenuus "native, freeborn," hence "noble, frank."

examples.text: It would be a unique delight to wait and watch for the melodious fragments in which her heart and soul came forth so directly and ingenuously.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He rose with a start, his ingenuous face looking as though it had been dipped in crimson: even the reddish tint in his beard seemed to deepen.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

examples.text: Nor did his blushes and awkwardness take away from it: she was pleased with these healthy tokens of the young gentleman's ingenuousness.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: Lacking flavor; lacking vigor or interest.
etymology: From Late Latin insipidus, from in- "not" + sapidus "tasty," from sapere "to taste, be wise" (also in "sapient").

examples.text: The eaters of the dinner, like the dinner itself, were lukewarm, insipid, overdone—and all owing to this poor little dull Young Barnacle.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: There it is before you—smiling, frowning, inviting, grand, mean, insipid, or savage, and always mute with an air of whispering, 'Come and find out.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The waves were colourless, and the Bournemouth steamer gave a further touch of insipidity, drawn up against the pier and hooting wildly for excursionists.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Unwilling or refusing to change one's views or to agree about something.
etymology: From Spanish los intransigentes, the name of an extreme republican party in the 1870s, from Latin in- "not" + transigere "to come to an agreement."

examples.text: Employers organization chairman, Jacques Schoufour, accused the FNV of intransigence in refusing to alter its stance at all over the past two months.
examples.source: Reuters, “Neither Side Optimistic On Rotterdam Port Issues”

examples.text: Jorge Cardenas, manager of the national federation and head of his nation's delegation in London, has blamed the intransigence of some big countries, without naming them.
examples.source: Reuters, “Colombia Coffee Exporters Believe In Pragmatism”

examples.text: Tesfay accused the West of intransigence in the negotiation of recent commodity agreements.
examples.source: Reuters, “Ethiopia Minister Sees Africa Debt Payment Problem”

definition: Fearless; adventurous.
etymology: From Latin intrepidus, from in- "not" + trepidus "alarmed" (compare "trepidation").

examples.text: She had thought that of course Tom had deserted long ago, and she wondered at seeing him place himself in her power again in this intrepid way.
examples.author: Mark Twain

examples.text: It spoke in a voice harsh and lugubrious but intrepid, and little by little it dawned upon Archie that this was a development of the Patna case.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: The brilliant Lady Stunnington tried a passage of arms with her, but was routed with great slaughter by the intrepid little Becky.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: To flood; to overwhelm someone with things to be dealt with.
etymology: From Latin inundare, from in- "onto" + unda "a wave."

examples.text: Here and there, especially at first, the inundation started on them and swept by; but when they had done descending, and were winding and climbing up a tower, they were alone.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Its air is much more attenuated than ours, its oceans have shrunk until they cover but a third of its surface, and as its slow seasons change huge snowcaps gather and melt about either pole and periodically inundate its temperate zones.
examples.author: H. G. Wells

examples.text: "We have the beer, but distribution and sales is the important point," van Schaik said, adding that since the ruling Heineken had been inundated by German traders seeking joint ventures.
examples.source: Reuters, “Heineken Sees Higher Profits, Wider Penetration”

definition: Using very few words.
etymology: From Greek Lakōnikos "of Laconia," the region around Sparta. Spartans were famed for curt speech; when Philip II of Macedon threatened "If I invade Laconia...," they reportedly replied, "If."

examples.text: Jude did not pause to remember that, in the laconic words of the historian, "insulted Nature sometimes vindicated her rights" in such circumstances.
examples.author: Thomas Hardy

examples.text: But their father, though very laconic in his expressions of pleasure, was really glad to see them; he had felt their importance in the family circle.
examples.author: Jane Austen

examples.text: Mr Plornish, as being of a more laconic temperament, embraced this opportunity of interposing with the suggestion that she should now leave Mr Clennam to himself.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

definition: Displaying or having a disinclination for physical exertion; relaxed and slow; weak or faint.
etymology: From Latin languidus "faint, weak," from languere "to be weak."

examples.text: It was not a scorching, hard, dusty day like the treacherous intruder of a week before, but soaked with languor, softened with a milky light.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: The wind shook some blossoms from the trees, and the heavy lilac-blooms, with their clustering stars, moved to and fro in the languid air.
examples.author: Oscar Wilde

examples.text: Quitting all languor Lionel cried in grief, in cry of passion dominant to love to return with deepening yet with rising chords of harmony.
examples.author: James Joyce

definition: Affected by a lack of energy or enthusiasm; sluggish.
etymology: From Greek lēthargos "forgetful," from lēthē "forgetfulness." Lethe was the river of forgetting in the underworld.

examples.text: The gaunt rooms, deserted for years upon years, seemed to have settled down into a gloomy lethargy from which nothing could rouse them again.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: The lethargy grows upon her, and though she seems strong and well, and is getting back some of her colour, Van Helsing and I are not satisfied.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: The French primary bond market is showing signs of renewed effervescence after several weeks of lethargy and the trend is expected to continue if hopes of imminent interest rate cuts are fulfilled, market operators said.
examples.source: Reuters, “French Primary Bond Market Shows New Sparkle”

definition: Tending to talk a great deal; talkative.
etymology: From Latin loquax "talkative," from loqui "to speak."

examples.text: They began to talk, and finding Clutton more loquacious and less sardonic than usual, Philip determined to take advantage of his good humour.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: Uncle Glegg stood open-mouthed with astonishment at this unembarrassed loquacity, with which his understanding could hardly keep pace.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Sancho Panza, who was wishing the goatherd's loquacity at the devil, on his part begged his master to go into Pedro's hut to sleep.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

definition: Expressed clearly and easy to understand; showing an ability to think clearly.
etymology: From Latin lucidus "bright," from lux "light."

examples.text: My dear lady," he lucidly pursued, "my work, you see, is really done, and my reasons for staying on even another day are none of the best.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: But he rode home with a terribly lucid vision of the difficulty there would be in arranging any result that could be permanently counted on with this man.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Him followed Rimmon, whose delightful seat Was fair Damascus, on the fertile banks Of Abbana and Pharphar, lucid streams.
examples.author: John Milton

definition: Very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.
etymology: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus "great" + animus "soul."

examples.text: I regard you in any case as a man of noble character and not without elements of magnanimity, though I don't agree with all your convictions.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: In spite of this magnanimity Dorothea was still smarting: perhaps as much from Celia's subdued astonishment as from her small criticisms.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: They have claims on the magnanimity and, I may add, on the justice of this nation which we must all feel.
examples.author: James Monroe

definition: A person who dislikes humankind and avoids human society.
etymology: From Greek misanthrōpos, from misein "to hate" + anthrōpos "human being." Popularized by Molière's play Le Misanthrope (1666).

examples.text: Like a plethoric burning martyr, or a self-consuming misanthrope, once ignited, the whale supplies his own fuel and burns by his own body.
examples.author: Herman Melville

examples.text: A perfect misanthropist's heaven: and Mr. Heathcliff and I are such a suitable pair to divide the desolation between us.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

examples.text: All the world used her ill, said this young misanthropist, and we may be pretty certain that persons whom all the world treats ill, deserve entirely the treatment they get.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

definition: To make something bad less severe, serious, or painful.
etymology: From Latin mitigare, from mitis "mild, soft" + agere "to make."

examples.text: Here also the firmness of the judicial magistracy is of vast importance in mitigating the severity and confining the operation of such laws.
examples.author: Hamilton

examples.text: We have not failed, nor shall we fail to respond, whenever necessary to mitigate human suffering and assist in the rehabilitation of distressed nations.
examples.author: Calvin Coolidge

examples.text: It said instead that such moves as increasing oil reserves and more exploration and development research would help to guard against or mitigate the risks of increased imports.
examples.source: Reuters, “Study Group Urges Increased U.S. Oil Reserves”

definition: To appease the anger or anxiety of someone.
etymology: From Latin mollificare "to soften," from mollis "soft."

examples.text: Analytical Chemist goes to the door, confers angrily with unseen tapper, appears to become mollified by descrying reason in the tapping, and goes out.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: "Dear, dear friend!" she said, with a touch of such natural feeling, that Miss Briggs of course at once began to melt, and even the bathing-woman was mollified.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: But some analysts said Japan's attempt to mollify the U.S. was a double edged sword, and might be read at a subtle form of trade retaliation for the tariffs proposed by the U.S.
examples.source: Reuters, “Japan Cuts Chip Supply, May Produce Shortage”

definition: Sullen and ill-tempered.
etymology: From Latin morosus "peevish, fastidious," from mos "custom, manner." Being set in one's ways became being sour about it.

examples.text: Ferguson appeared to be a morose and silent man, but I could see from the little that he said that he was at least a fellow-countryman.
examples.author: Arthur Conan Doyle

examples.text: The count ordered his carriage that he might drive to Sokolniki, and sat in his study with folded hands, morose, sallow, and taciturn.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: Dorset, of late, had grown more than usually morose and incalculable, and Ned Silverton went about with an air that seemed to challenge the universe.
examples.author: Edith Wharton

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action.
etymology: From Latin obdurare "to harden," from ob- "against" + durus "hard."

examples.text: This old man wears a hat, a thumbed and napless and yet an obdurate hat, which has never adapted itself to the shape of his poor head.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: May I die if the enchanters that persecute me are not trying to entangle me in them and delay my journey, by way of revenge for my obduracy towards Altisidora.
examples.author: Miguel de Cervantes (tr. John Ormsby)

examples.text: She came, but refused to kiss them: it was such hard luck on the little things, she said, and though Dolly proffered Chorly-worly and Porgly-woggles in turn, she was obdurate.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: Obedient or attentive to an excessive or servile degree.
etymology: From Latin obsequiosus "compliant," from obsequi "to comply," from ob- "toward" + sequi "to follow."

examples.text: Philip flushed, all the more because the surgeon spoke obviously with a humorous intention, and his brow-beaten dressers laughed obsequiously.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: The cavalcade passed out by the lower gate of Phoenix park saluted by obsequious policemen and proceeded past Kingsbridge along the northern quays.
examples.author: James Joyce

examples.text: Babbitt's porter was an obsequious gray-haired negro who did him an honor highly esteemed in the land of Zenith—greeted him by name.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or chosen course of action, despite attempts to persuade.
etymology: From Latin obstinatus "determined," from obstinare "to persist."

examples.text: With regard to a large number of matters about which other men are decided or obstinate, he was the most easily manageable man in the world.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: He always took her hand as though with repugnance, always seemed vexed to meet her and was sometimes obstinately silent throughout her visit.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: The money market head said the unions' humiliation by the protracted financial problems of the Neue Heimat cooperative housing venture would contribute to union obstinacy.
examples.source: Reuters, “German Wage Round Said To Limit Monetary Options”

definition: To remove a need or difficulty; to avoid or prevent.
etymology: From Late Latin obviare "to meet in the way, prevent," from ob viam "in the way."

examples.text: The propositions which have been made for supplying the omission have rather served to illustrate than to obviate the difficulty of the thing.
examples.author: Hamilton

examples.text: In order to obviate any delays possible through any routine requirements as to payment in your departments, we enclose cheque herewith for ten pounds (L10), receipt of which please acknowledge.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: Having approached this structure, I looked inside, and perceived it to be a singular sort of old-fashioned couch, very conveniently designed to obviate the necessity for every member of the family having a room to himself.
examples.author: Emily Brontë

definition: Assertive of authority in an annoyingly domineering way, especially about trivial matters; meddlesome.
etymology: From Latin officiosus "obliging, dutiful," from officium "service, duty." Being eager to serve tipped into meddling.

examples.text: Margaret Schlegel has been officious and tiresome during this terrible week, and we have all suffered under her, but upon my soul she's honest.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

examples.text: You don't know how the cursed carelessness that is over-officious in helping me at every other turning of my life, WON'T help me here.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: How this charmingly convenient obstacle could have escaped the officious penetration of the Count, it was impossible to conceive—but it HAD escaped him.
examples.author: Wilkie Collins

definition: Involving a great deal of effort, trouble, or difficulty; burdensome.
etymology: From Latin onerosus, from onus "a load, burden."

examples.text: I think on the whole the bishop was right, for though the services required will not be of a very onerous nature, they will be more so than they were before.
examples.author: Anthony Trollope

examples.text: And Boris, having apparently relieved himself of an onerous duty and extricated himself from an awkward situation and placed another in it, became quite pleasant again.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude)

examples.text: The appointing power vested in the President imposes delicate and onerous duties.
examples.author: Zachary Taylor

definition: Characterized by vulgar or pretentious display, designed to impress.
etymology: From Latin ostentare "to display," frequentative of ostendere "to show."

examples.text: He carried his fat paunch with ostentation on his short legs, and during the time his gang infested the station spoke to no one but his nephew.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: Our honesty, we free spirits—let us be careful lest it become our vanity, our ornament and ostentation, our limitation, our stupidity!
examples.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (tr. Helen Zimmern)

examples.text: Her husband was lying in a great leather chair in the dining-room, and by his side, holding his hand rather ostentatiously, was Evie.
examples.author: E. M. Forster

definition: A person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a particular quality.
etymology: From Italian paragone "touchstone," a stone used to test the purity of gold, from Greek parakonan "to sharpen against."

examples.text: Down in Bleeding Heart Yard, where there was not one unappropriated halfpenny, as lively an interest was taken in this paragon of men as on the Stock Exchange.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: From heaven the hero must be smiling down upon that paragon of a boy whom he had left to comfort and console her.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: Paragon said it bought the shares for investment purposes.

definition: The presence of something in only small or insufficient quantities.
etymology: From Latin paucitas, from paucus "few" (related to "paltry" and "poor").

examples.text: Any inward debate Lydgate had as to the consequences of this engagement which had stolen upon him, turned on the paucity of time rather than of money.
examples.author: George Eliot

examples.text: Here again I found the tally agreeing exactly; the carriers' men were able to supplement the paucity of the written words with a few details.
examples.author: Bram Stoker

examples.text: Nashashibi said lack of experience among Arab banks, a paucity of financial instruments and a legal framework that often does not recognise the western banking concept of interest have hampered the growth of Arab markets.
examples.source: Reuters, “Arab Banker Says Too Soon For Single Currency”

definition: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules; overscrupulous.
etymology: From Italian pedante "teacher, schoolmaster," perhaps from Greek paideuein "to teach."

examples.text: If he was to get away because of some of the relations involved in staying, the cold attitude toward them might look pedantic in the light of lingering on.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: His gentleness was never tinged by dogmatism, and his instructions were given with an air of frankness and good nature that banished every idea of pedantry.
examples.author: Mary Shelley

examples.text: Not for scoundrels, but for pedantic poseurs, 'haunted by profound, unsolved doubts.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)

definition: Carried out with a minimum of effort or reflection, merely as a routine duty.
etymology: From Late Latin perfunctorius "careless," from perfungi "to get through with, discharge."

examples.text: Now and again he would emit a bothered perfunctory "Sssh," which neither produced nor was expected to produce the slightest effect.
examples.author: Joseph Conrad

examples.text: She had invented a way of meeting them—as if he had been a polite perfunctory poor relation, of distant degree—that made them almost ridiculous in him.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: Reforms in the civil service must go on; but the changes should be real and genuine, not perfunctory, or prompted by a zeal in behalf of any party simply because it happens to be in power.
examples.author: William McKinley

definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.
etymology: From Latin perniciosus "destructive," from pernicies "ruin," from per- "completely" + nex "death."

examples.text: Despite that pernicious assumption of lassitude and indifference, which had become his second nature, he was strongly attached to his friend.
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: Sviazhsky began talking of Levin, describing his strange view that machinery is simply pernicious in its effects on Russian agriculture.
examples.author: Leo Tolstoy (tr. Constance Garnett)

examples.text: It will furnish absolute security which makes the proposed scheme of government guaranty of deposits so alluring, without its pernicious results.
examples.author: William Howard Taft

definition: To make someone less angry or hostile.
etymology: From Latin placare "to soothe," related to placere "to please."

examples.text: His manner of sneering at what he called "parlor socialists" (though the phrase was not overwhelmingly new) had a power which made her wish to placate his company of well-fed, speed-loving administrators.
examples.author: Sinclair Lewis

examples.text: For the rest of the term he tormented Philip cruelly, and, though Philip tried to keep out of his way, the school was so small that it was impossible; he tried being friendly and jolly with him; he abased himself, so far as to buy him a knife; but though Singer took the knife he was not placated.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

examples.text: But today's smaller than expected rate cut appeared to have placated markets for now, analysts said.
examples.source: Reuters, “U.K. Base Rates Will Fall Again Soon, Say Analysts”

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically, based on practical rather than theoretical considerations.
etymology: From Greek pragmatikos "relating to affairs," from pragma "deed, thing done."

examples.text: They represent a pragmatic rededication to social compassion and national excellence, in place of the combination of good intentions and fuzzy follow-through which too often in the past was thought sufficient.
examples.author: Richard Nixon

examples.text: Arango said that government measures adopted here last week, including a lower export registration price, indicated a major change but also disclosed a welcome pragmatism.
examples.source: Reuters, “Colombia Coffee Exporters Believe In Pragmatism”

examples.text: An economist at a German bank, who declined to be identified, said "If Poehl is confirmed in his post, it will certainly be a plus for the pragmatic course which is not so rigidly oriented towards money supply."
examples.source: Reuters, “Poehl Looks Set For Eight More Years At Bundesbank”

definition: To speak or act in an evasive way; to avoid telling the whole truth.
etymology: From Latin praevaricari "to walk crookedly," from prae- "before" + varicare "to straddle," from varus "bent, knock-kneed."

examples.text: Barbara denied, prevaricated, stammered, and at last was overcome with confusion; for which even the most indulgent spectators could scarcely pity her.
examples.author: Maria Edgeworth

examples.text: It was nevertheless no light matter that the very effect of his confusion should be to make him again prevaricate.
examples.author: Henry James

examples.text: The bubble of frustration against what appears as Japanese prevarication burst last week.
examples.source: Reuters, “Japan Isolated, Yen Rises, World Feels Cheated”

definition: In its original condition; unspoiled; clean and fresh as if new.
etymology: From Latin pristinus "former, early." The sense "spotless, new" developed only in the 20th century.

examples.text: And the separation is essential to the preservation of that institution in its pristine purity.
examples.author: Hamilton

examples.text: It grovelled helpless on the ground, even while his intellectual faculties retained their pristine strength, or had perhaps acquired a morbid energy, which disease only could have given them.
examples.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

examples.text: When the genuine spirit of liberty animates the body of a people to a thorough examination of their affairs, it leads to the excision of every excrescence which may have fastened itself upon any of the departments of the government, and restores the system to its pristine health and beauty.
examples.author: William Henry Harrison

definition: Spending money or resources freely and recklessly; wastefully extravagant. As a noun, a person who leaves and returns repentant.
etymology: From Latin prodigus "wasteful," from prodigere "to drive away, squander." The Prodigal Son parable (Luke 15) gave the noun sense.

examples.text: I have not seen my mother this long time, and it lies upon my conscience, for it's something to be loved as she loves her prodigal son.—-Bah!
examples.author: Charles Dickens

examples.text: At this festival the magnificence displayed was such as had not been known in the little German place since the days of the prodigal Victor XIV.
examples.author: William Makepeace Thackeray

examples.text: The toleration of this idea results in the waste of the people's money by their chosen servants and encourages prodigality and extravagance in the home life of our countrymen.
examples.author: Grover Cleveland

definition: Recklessly extravagant or wasteful; licentious, dissolute.
etymology: From Latin profligatus "ruined, dissolute," from profligare "to strike down."

examples.text: Then followed a paragraph giving other examples of such heroes and Saviours being born of some profligate intercourse between God and mortal.
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton

examples.text: These were the very words of the old profligate, who felt already that his death was not far off and who actually died five months later.
examples.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky (tr. Constance Garnett)
